\chapter{The Bracket}
\label{ch:ge-klammer}
\hlchaptermodality{51}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say what I can, must and would like to do, hold the second verb until the end of the sentence, and build both families of past participle.}

Every verb in the book is put inside a bracket, and then the seven preceding chapters are run in one breath over one small set of nouns. The chapter names a habit the reader has met three times already -- a separable prefix, a past participle and a nicht that cancels a verb all go to the same last slot -- so the modal bracket arrives as the fourth instance of one rule rather than a fourth rule.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[können]{können — \textquotedblleft{}can,\textquotedblright{} and the verb that meant \emph{know}}

\label{lesson:GE-C38-koennen}



\begin{quote}
The simple-past chapter gave you \textbf{konnte}, \textquotedblleft{}could\textquotedblright{}. You have been able to say what you could do and not what you can do, which is an odd way round. This lesson fixes it.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} two chapters back, the four possessives — \emph{mein, dein, sein, ihr}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: können}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{können} — \textquotedblleft{}to be able\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}can\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich kann.} — \textquotedblleft{}I can.\textquotedblright{} · \textbf{Du kannst.} — \textquotedblleft{}You can.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Notice the \emph{ich} form. It is \textbf{kann}, not \emph{könne}: this verb takes no ending at all in the first person, and its vowel changes as well. A small closed family of German verbs behaves like this, and every one of them is a word you will say constantly — which is the usual bargain, since the commonest words are the ones worn irregular by use.

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich kann Deutsch.} — \textquotedblleft{}I can speak German\textquotedblright{}, with no second verb at all.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{können} and English \textbf{can} are one word, and both began as a word for \textbf{knowing}. The root is Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*ǵneh\textsubscript{3}-}}, which also gave English \textbf{know}, Scots \textbf{ken}, Latin \textbf{nōscō} and Greek \textbf{gnosis}.

So \emph{I can} once meant \emph{I know how}, and the drift from knowledge to ability happened before English and German separated. That is why \emph{ich kann Deutsch} — \textquotedblleft{}I know German\textquotedblright{} — still sounds entirely ordinary with no verb after it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich kann.\textquotedblright{} then \textquotedblleft{}Du kannst.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair with the past you already had — \textquotedblleft{}Ich kann\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Ich konnte\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich kann Deutsch.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the old meaning, out loud — \emph{can} was \emph{know}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich kann Deutsch.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is the \emph{ich} form of \emph{können}? (\emph{\textbf{Kann}} — no ending, and a changed vowel.) What did the word mean before it meant \emph{be able}? (\textbf{To know} — the root behind \emph{know} and \emph{ken}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}I can speak German\textquotedblright{} without a second verb. (\textbf{Ich kann Deutsch.})
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[möchten]{möchten — \textquotedblleft{}I would like,\textquotedblright{} the politest verb in the book}

\label{lesson:GE-C38-moechten}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Mögen} is yours, and so is \textbf{bitte}. Between them you can say what you like and you can say please, and you still cannot order a coffee.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: möchten}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{möchten} — \textquotedblleft{}would like\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.} — \textquotedblleft{}I'd like a coffee, please.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

That sentence is the single most useful one in this chapter, and every piece of it is already yours except the verb: the \emph{einen} from the having lessons, the \emph{bitte} from the requests lesson, and the \emph{Kaffee} from the drinks chapter.

Like \emph{kann}, the \emph{ich} form takes no ending: \textbf{ich möchte}, \textbf{du möchtest}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{möchten} is \textbf{mögen} with its vowel bent — the umlaut doing grammatical work again, as it has done in every plural that took one. The bent form is historically a \emph{past} shape pressed into service for the present, and that is precisely what makes it polite.

English runs the identical trick and nobody notices:

\begin{quote}
\emph{I \textbf{will} have a coffee} $\to$ \emph{I \textbf{would} like a coffee} \emph{\textbf{Can} you help} $\to$ \emph{\textbf{Could} you help}
\end{quote}

A past-shaped verb standing in the present puts a little distance between the speaker and the demand. Both languages found the same politeness strategy, and German marks it with two dots.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte einen Tee, bitte.\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte Wasser, bitte.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the blunt one, then the polite one — \textquotedblleft{}Ich mag Kaffee\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte einen Kaffee\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two modals so far — \textquotedblleft{}ich kann, ich möchte\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte einen Kaffee, bitte.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which verb is \emph{möchten} a bent form of? (\emph{\textbf{Mögen}}.) What is the bend doing? (\textbf{Making it polite} — a past-shaped form used in the present.) Which English pair does the same? (\emph{\textbf{Will}} and \emph{\textbf{would}}.) Order a coffee.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[müssen]{müssen — \textquotedblleft{}must,\textquotedblright{} and the ending that is missing in both languages}

\label{lesson:GE-C38-muessen}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{ich kann} and \textbf{ich möchte}. Neither took the \emph{-e} that ordinary verbs take. Say \textbf{er wohnt} and hear the \emph{-t} that ordinary verbs do take, and then watch the third modal do without it too.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: müssen}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{müssen} — \textquotedblleft{}to have to\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}must\textquotedblright{}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich muss.} · \textbf{Du musst.} · \textbf{Er muss.}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{ich} form and the \textbf{er} form are identical, and both are bare. That is the mark of this small family: no \emph{-e}, no \emph{-t}, and a vowel that changes.

\begin{cousinweb}
English has exactly the same hole, in exactly the same words, and every English speaker has been ignoring it for life:

\begin{quote}
\emph{he walk\textbf{s}}, \emph{he live\textbf{s}}, \emph{he think\textbf{s}} — but \emph{he \textbf{must}}, \emph{he \textbf{can}}, \emph{he \textbf{may}}, with no \emph{-s} at all.
\end{quote}

The reason is one accident, eight hundred years old and shared. This handful of verbs were once \textbf{past tenses}, and a past tense took no ending in the present because it was not a present. They then drifted into meaning present things and kept their bare shape.

So the missing \emph{-t} in \emph{er muss} and the missing \emph{-s} in \emph{he must} are the same missing ending, and if the English one has never bothered you, the German one need not either.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich muss.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Du musst.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Er muss.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three modals — \textquotedblleft{}ich kann, ich möchte, ich muss\textquotedblright{}
  \item an ordinary verb beside them — \textquotedblleft{}er wohnt\textquotedblright{} against \textquotedblleft{}er muss\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English hole out loud — \textquotedblleft{}he walks\textquotedblright{} against \textquotedblleft{}he must\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich kann, ich möchte, ich muss.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What ending does \emph{er muss} take? (\textbf{None} — and neither does \emph{er kann}.) Which English verbs have the same hole? (\emph{\textbf{Must, can, may}} — no \emph{-s}.) Why? (\textbf{They were past tenses once}, and a past tense took no present ending.) Next: where the second verb goes.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[die Verbklammer]{die Verbklammer — the bracket German has been building all along}

\label{lesson:GE-C38-klammer}



\begin{quote}
Name three things this book has already sent to the end of a German sentence. Take your time; you have met all three.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the modal holds slot two, the other verb waits at the end}]
\begin{quote}
A modal takes slot two, and the verb it governs goes \textbf{last}, in its dictionary form.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.} — \textquotedblleft{}I can speak German.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich muss Deutsch lernen.} — \textquotedblleft{}I must learn German.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ich möchte einen Kaffee trinken.} — \textquotedblleft{}I'd like to drink a coffee.\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

Two verbs, one at each end, and everything the sentence is about held between them. German grammarians call that shape a \textbf{Klammer}, a bracket, and it is the skeleton of an ordinary German sentence.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{culture}
This is not a new rule. It is the fourth appearance of one habit, and the four were taught chapters apart:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{separable prefix} goes to the end — \emph{ich mache die Tür auf};
  \item a \textbf{past participle} goes to the end — \emph{ich habe Deutsch gelernt};
  \item \textbf{nicht} goes to the end when it cancels the verb — \emph{ich verstehe nicht};
  \item and now an \textbf{infinitive} goes to the end after a modal.
\end{itemize}

Four different pieces, one position. German reserves the last slot of a sentence for whatever completes the sense, and asks its listener to wait. That is the single most-remarked feature of the language, and by the time it is named here you have already met three quarters of it.
\end{culture}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say the modal, then hold the second verb until the end.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich kann Deutsch lernen.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich muss schlafen.\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte gehen.\textquotedblright{}
  \item with the verbs of the page — \textquotedblleft{}Ich kann lesen. Ich kann schreiben.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte dir helfen.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the four things that go last — a prefix, a participle, \emph{nicht}, an infinitive
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich muss Deutsch lernen.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Where does the modal stand, and where does the other verb stand? (\textbf{Slot two, and last.}) In what form is the second verb? (\textbf{The dictionary form.}) Name the four things German sends to the end of a sentence. Next: the participle that ends in \emph{-en}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[gegangen]{gegangen — the other half of the past}

\label{lesson:GE-C38-partizip-en}



\begin{quote}
Say \textbf{ich habe gelernt}. The participle is wrapped in \textbf{ge-} and ends in \textbf{-t}, which the past chapter taught. Now say \textbf{ich bin gegangen} — which you have also said, and which ends in something else entirely.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the second family ends in -en}]
\begin{quote}
German builds participles two ways. The weak family wraps the stem in \textbf{ge-} and \textbf{-t}. The strong family wraps it in \textbf{ge-} and \textbf{-en}, and very often changes the vowel as well.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{gehen $\to$ gegangen} · \textbf{sehen $\to$ gesehen} · \textbf{lesen $\to$ gelesen} · \textbf{schreiben $\to$ geschrieben}
\end{quote}

The \textbf{ge-} is the same unstressed wrapper in both families, so half of every participle in the language is already yours. What the strong family adds is the \textbf{-en} ending and a vowel that may move — and the moving vowel is the same strong-verb behaviour that gave you \emph{du liest} and \emph{du siehst}.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
English split its participles the same way, into the same two shapes, and every English speaker sorts them without thinking:

\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{weak} & \textbf{strong} \\
\midrule
walk\textbf{ed}, learn\textbf{ed}, ask\textbf{ed} & go\textbf{ne}, see\textbf{n}, writt\textbf{en}, giv\textbf{en} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

That \emph{-en} on \emph{given} and \emph{written} is German's \emph{-en} on \emph{gegeben} and \emph{geschrieben} — the same ending, in the same job, inherited rather than borrowed. English then lost the \emph{ge-} wrapper, which German kept, so the German participle is the fuller survival of a shape both languages had.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say the dictionary form, then wrap it.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}gehen $\to$ gegangen\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}sehen $\to$ gesehen\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lesen $\to$ gelesen\textquotedblright{}, \textquotedblleft{}schreiben $\to$ geschrieben\textquotedblright{}
  \item the weak family beside it — \textquotedblleft{}gelernt, gesagt, gemacht\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two helpers with the two families — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe gelesen.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin gegangen.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the English pair that proves the split — \textquotedblleft{}walked\textquotedblright{} against \textquotedblleft{}written\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe gelesen. Ich bin gegangen.\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the two participle endings? (\emph{\textbf{-t}} for the weak family, \emph{\textbf{-en}} for the strong.) What do both families share? (\textbf{The \emph{ge-} wrapper}, never stressed.) Which English participles end in \emph{-en}? (\emph{\textbf{Gone, seen, written, given}} — the same family, the same ending.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Was kann ich? — the chapter, and the seven before it, run cold}

\label{lesson:GE-R38-was-kann-ich}



\begin{quote}
Name the four things German sends to the end of a sentence. Then say the two participle endings and what both families share.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: the bracket over every verb}
Every verb the book owns, held at the end of a bracket. Say the modal first and make yourself wait for the second verb.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich kann lesen, schreiben, hören, sehen.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich muss schlafen, gehen, laufen, lernen.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte fragen, helfen, nehmen.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the pair that opens and closes — \textquotedblleft{}Ich muss die Tür öffnen. Ich muss die Tür schließen.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two of rest — \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte sitzen. Ich möchte stehen.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the chapter's own sentence — \textquotedblleft{}Ich kann Deutsch lernen.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the distant band — eight chapters in one breath}
Everything the last seven chapters bought, in order, over one small set of nouns.

Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item negation — \textquotedblleft{}Ich habe keinen Hund. Ich verstehe nicht.\textquotedblright{}
  \item a question and a command — \textquotedblleft{}Hast du einen Hund?\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Komm!\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three new W-words — \textquotedblleft{}Wer? Wann? Warum?\textquotedblright{}
  \item which and how many — \textquotedblleft{}Welcher Hund? Wie viele Hunde?\textquotedblright{}
  \item the marked row and existence — \textquotedblleft{}Ich sehe den Hund. Es gibt keinen Kaffee.\textquotedblright{}
  \item an adjective that stays still — \textquotedblleft{}Der Kaffee ist gut.\textquotedblright{}
  \item two joined thoughts, both ways — \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte Kaffee, aber ich habe keine Zeit.\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}Ich bin müde, weil ich keine Zeit habe.\textquotedblright{}
  \item whose, and who — \textquotedblleft{}Das ist mein Bruder. Das ist sein Hund.\textquotedblright{}
  \item the done-to row — \textquotedblleft{}Ich sehe ihn. Ich sehe dich. Ich sehe euch.\textquotedblright{}
  \item bent back — \textquotedblleft{}Er wäscht sich.\textquotedblright{}
  \item and all of it in one sentence — \textquotedblleft{}Ich möchte meinen Bruder fragen, weil ich ihn nicht verstehe.\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say the three modals. (\emph{\textbf{Kann, möchte, muss}} — none of them with an ending.) Where does the second verb go, and in what form? (\textbf{Last, in the dictionary form.}) Name the four things German sends to that same last slot. (\textbf{A separable prefix, a past participle, the \emph{nicht} that cancels a verb, and an infinitive after a modal.}) And which participle ending marks the strong family? (\emph{\textbf{-en}}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
